Description_Simple.comparison_text:
Title: Top K Frequent Elements in a 2D Array

Main Goal: Given a two-dimensional array of numbers (nums) and an integer k, the code finds the k numbers that appear most frequently across all subarrays.

How it works:
1. It first builds a frequency map (d) counting occurrences of each number.
2. Defines a MinHeap class of fixed capacity k to keep track of the k highest frequencies:
   - When adding a (frequency, number) pair, if the heap has fewer than k elements, it simply inserts it.
   - Otherwise, it compares the new frequency to the heap’s minimum; if larger, it replaces the min.
3. After processing all entries in the frequency map, it extracts the numbers from the heap (the k most frequent) into the result array.
4. Returns the list of those k most frequent numbers.

Description_Simple.reference_text: Write a function to find k number of pairs which consist of one element from the first array and one element from the second array.
Description_Simple.comparison_text:
Title: Finding the k Smallest Sum Pairs with a Min Heap

Main Goal: Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2, the code returns the k pairs (one element from each array) whose sums are the smallest.

Short Summary:
1. MinHeap class:
   - Implements a binary min‐heap of [sum, i, j] tuples.
   - push(val) adds an element and restores heap order via _siftUp.
   - pop() removes and returns the smallest element (root), then restores order via _siftDown.
2. kSmallestPairs(nums1, nums2, k):
   - Uses the heap to explore pair sums in ascending order without generating all pairs.
   - Starts by pushing the (0,0) pair.
   - Repeatedly pops the smallest sum tuple [sum, i, j], records the pair [nums1[i], nums2[j]], then:
     a. Pushes the next pair in nums2: (i, j+1).
     b. If at the start of a row (j===0), also pushes the next pair in nums1: (i+1, 0).
   - Stops when k pairs are collected or heap is empty.
This yields the k pairs with the smallest possible sums efficiently in O(k log k) time.

Title: Obfuscated JavaScript “isIsomorphic” Function

Main Goal: After running through several layers of base-64 and RC4-style decoding, this code ultimately defines and exports a function named `isIsomorphic(s, t)` that checks whether two input strings `s` and `t` are isomorphic (i.e. there is a one-to-one character mapping from `s` to `t`). 

Summary Description:
The snippet is a heavily obfuscated implementation of the classic “isomorphic strings” algorithm. It begins by shuffling and decoding a hidden array of strings via two helper functions (`_0xfcde` and `_0x4bf6`) that perform Base64+URL decoding and an RC4-style decryption respectively. These helpers supply the real property names and constant values used later on. After the self-invoking anti-tamper loop runs, the code defines:

function isIsomorphic(s, t) {
  • Build a map from each character in s to a list of its positions.
  • Build a map from each character in t to a list of its positions.
  • Extract the position-lists from both maps, sort them by key, flatten to arrays.
  • Return true if the two flattened arrays have the same length and identical entries at each index; false otherwise.
}

In short, the entire obfuscation layer serves only to conceal a straightforward routine that determines whether two strings are isomorphic.

Description:

Title: Maximum Sum with No Three Consecutive Elements

Main Goal:  
This function computes the largest possible sum of values from an input array under the constraint that you cannot include three consecutive elements in the chosen sum. It uses dynamic programming (the `dp` array) to track, for each index `i`, the best sum achievable up to that position without ever taking three in a row.

How It Works:
1. Initialize a `dp` array where `dp[i]` represents the maximum valid sum considering elements `0` through `i`.  
2. Seed the base cases for `i = 0, 1, 2`, handling very small arrays directly.  
3. For each index `i ≥ 3`, compute `dp[i]` as the maximum of:  
   • Skipping `arr[i]` → `dp[i-1]`  
   • Taking `arr[i]` alone (thus skipping `arr[i-1]`) → `dp[i-2] + arr[i]`  
   • Taking both `arr[i]` and `arr[i-1]` (thus skipping `arr[i-2]`) → `dp[i-3] + arr[i-1] + arr[i]`  
4. Return `dp[n-1]`, the best sum for the entire array length `n`.

Main Goal:
Given a non-negative integer n, the function locates the highest-order bit that is currently 0 (i.e., the leftmost unset bit in its binary form) and returns a new integer with that bit flipped to 1. If n’s binary representation is already all 1s (so there is no unset bit below its most significant bit), it returns n unchanged.

Explanation:

3. After the scan, the stored index corresponds to the most significant 0 bit encountered. The function sets that bit by OR-ing n with 1 shifted left by that index and returns the result.

Explanation:

Main goal: This code employs obfuscation and runtime decryption routines to hide its logic, but its core purpose is to provide a function (intToRoman) that converts a positive integer into its corresponding Roman numeral string.

Key components:
1. _0x3db0, _0x5de7, _0x2f98: Helper functions that manage an array of encoded strings, perform Base64/percent decoding, and apply a simple RC4-like cipher. These are used purely to obscure literal values and control flow.

Title: Rightmost Bit Manipulation Utilities

Main Goal:  
Provide two helper functions—one to find the position of the lowest set bit in a given integer, and another to flip its lowest unset (zero) bit to 1, handling edge cases (n=0 or all bits set).

Functions:
1. getPosOfRightMostSetBit(n):  
   - Isolates the least significant 1-bit via n & -n  
   - Returns its 1-based index using log2

2. setRightMostUnsetBit(n):  
   - If n=0, returns 1  
   - If n has no zero bits (all lower bits are 1), returns n unchanged  
   - Otherwise finds the lowest zero bit (using getPosOfRightMostSetBit(~n)) and sets it to 1

### Title
Obfuscated String Decryption with a Simple Regex Validator

Main goal  
This code is heavily obfuscated but ultimately implements a utility function named `textMatchTwoThree` that tests whether an input string matches the regular expression `/ab{2,3}/` (i.e. an “a” followed by two or three “b” characters). • The decryption functions cache their results so each string is decrypted only once.

Title: Obfuscated String Decryption and Regex Matching

Main goal: This snippet implements a lightweight runtime deobfuscation engine. Title: Obfuscated “starts with a, ends with b” Checker

Main goal: Define a function text_starta_endb that tests whether a given string matches the pattern “start with ‘a’ and end with ‘b’” and returns one of two hidden messages.

Description:
- The top‐level IIFE and the two helper functions (_0x32ad and _0x32f3) implement an anti-tamper/anti-debug array shuffling and a pair of decoders (Base64+URL-decode and RC4+Base64+URL-decode) to hide all real string literals.
- The array _0x463e() holds the obfuscated string constants.
- The function text_starta_endb(input) uses the regex /a.*?b$/ to test the input. If it matches, it returns one decoded string; otherwise it returns another decoded string. The actual messages are recovered at runtime via the hidden decoders.

Description_Simple.comparison_text:
Title: Obfuscated String Decoder and Text Matcher

Main Goal:  
This snippet hides all its string literals behind heavy obfuscation (array shuffling, Base64/percent-decoding, RC4) and exposes a single API, `textMatch`, which tests an input string against the regex `/ab*?/` and returns one of two secret messages decoded at runtime.

Functions:  
• _0x5a4c: Returns the array of encoded strings.  
• _0xa03c: Base64-plus-percent-decoding routine with memoization for one set of strings.  
• _0x4008: RC4 cipher decoder with memoization for another set of strings.  
• IIFE (immediately-invoked function): Rotates the string array until a numeric checksum matches, complicating static analysis.  
• textMatch(input): Applies `/ab*?/`. If true, returns the first hidden message (via _0xa03c); otherwise returns the second (via _0xa03c).
